title: Iran condemns US plans to announce new sanctions
gist: Nearly six months into the US-Israel war with Iran, Washington is preparing what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calls the 'toughest sanctions in history,' Strait of Hormuz oil flow has collapsed to roughly 40% of pre-war volume, and both sides show contradictory signals of defiance and openness to a deal.

themes.theme: New US sanctions push and secondary-sanctions risk

insights.claim: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is scheduled to hold a press conference on Monday at 2 p.m. EDT to announce new sanctions on Iran that he has described as the toughest in history.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: A concrete announcement date gives traders a hard catalyst for Iran-exposed shipping, insurance and China-Iran oil trade names; position ahead of the Monday 1800 GMT presser.
insights.quote: threatening "the toughest sanctions in history" on Iran
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent'

insights.claim: China buys more than 80% of Iran's shipped oil, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler, making Beijing the pivotal actor in whether new US secondary sanctions on Iran actually bite.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Sanctions efficacy hinges almost entirely on Chinese compliance; if Beijing continues 'urging diplomacy' rather than complying, expect the sanctions to be more symbolic than binding on actual Iranian oil export volumes.
insights.quote: China, which buys more than 80% of Iran's shipped oil, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler
insights.locator: paragraph on Bessent urging China cooperation

insights.claim: Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei called the imminent US sanctions announcement an illegal assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over UN member states, signaling Tehran will not treat the sanctions as legitimate grounds for compliance.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Iran's rejection of the sanctions' legal basis foreshadows continued attempts to route trade through non-compliant partners (China) rather than negotiate; expect limited near-term sanctions-driven behavior change from Tehran.
insights.quote: Such secondary sanctions find no foundation in international law

insights.claim: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, warned that Tehran will treat any country that joins the US economic pressure campaign against Iran as an enemy.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: This is a direct threat aimed at Gulf and regional states weighing cooperation with US sanctions enforcement; raises geopolitical risk premium for any country seen aligning with Washington on Iran policy.
insights.quote: We are telling all nearby countries not to join the U.S. economic war, otherwise we will consider them as enemies
insights.locator: quote attributed to Rezaei on state television

insights.claim: President Trump said Washington was merely 'observing what happens' in the conflict and suggested Iran is not yet ready to accept terms he considers a fair deal.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Trump's wait-and-see posture combined with maximalist sanctions suggests the US strategy is economic attrition rather than an imminent return to direct negotiations, implying a longer runway of elevated Hormuz risk.
insights.quote: They would love to make a deal, but they're not ready to make the right deal, in my opinion

themes.theme: Strait of Hormuz oil flow collapse

insights.claim: Only four commodity ships sailed through the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, and none were large crude carriers or LNG tankers, indicating the strait is functionally closed to major energy cargo despite not being formally blockaded.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Near-total cessation of large crude/LNG transit through Hormuz is a massive supply shock; track global oil and LNG spot prices and freight/insurance rates for continued upside pressure as long as this persists.
insights.quote: Only four commodity ships sailed along the strait on Thursday, none of them large crude carriers or liquefied natural gas tankers, ship-tracking data showed.

insights.claim: US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the US military has helped move a seven-day average of 8 million barrels a day through the Strait of Hormuz, down from more than 20 million barrels a day before the war -- a roughly 60% collapse in flow through a corridor that once carried about one in every five barrels consumed worldwide.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: A ~60% drop in Hormuz throughput, even with US military escort, quantifies the real physical oil-supply damage from the war -- a key input for modeling sustained crude price floors and refiner margins.
insights.quote: the U.S. military helped move a seven-day average of 8 million barrels a day of oil through the strait. That's down from more than 20 million per day before the war or about one of every five barrels consumed worldwide.

insights.claim: Iran has granted special permission for a number of Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz after repeated requests from Baghdad, following a visit to Iraq by Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Selective Iranian carve-outs for Iraqi tankers show Tehran is willing to use strait access as a bargaining chip with individual neighbors, a mechanism that could be replicated for other partners willing to align regionally with Iran.
insights.locator: paragraph on Iraqi oil tankers granted passage

insights.claim: Despite US strikes severely damaging Iran's economy, navy and air force, Tehran retains enough missile and drone capability to continue impeding oil tanker traffic and threatening regional rivals.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Asymmetric missile/drone capability, not conventional naval strength, is what is actually driving the Hormuz shipping freeze -- meaning the disruption could persist even after Iran's conventional forces are further degraded.
insights.quote: U.S. attacks have severely diminished Iran's economy and devastated its navy and air force, but Tehran maintains enough missile and drone capability to impede oil tanker traffic and attack regional rivals.
insights.locator: paragraph before ballistic missile plant visit

insights.claim: Iran's armed forces chief of staff, Abdollahi, publicized a visit to an underground ballistic missile manufacturing plant, claiming production capacity, quality and quantity are now better than in the past.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: A public signal of resilient/improving domestic missile production undercuts the thesis that sanctions and strikes have crippled Iran's military-industrial base, and argues against assuming Hormuz risk fades quickly.
insights.quote: This plant has been able, much better than in the past, to produce equipment superior both in capacities and quality and in quantity
insights.locator: quote from Abdollahi on state television

insights.claim: Iran's parliamentary speaker Qalibaf said Tehran has received numerous messages from unnamed neighboring countries about establishing new regional security arrangements and economic cooperation outside the existing US-led order.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: An unverified claim of a forming 'homegrown' regional bloc is worth monitoring but should be treated as Iranian messaging/propaganda until specific countries and agreements are named.
insights.quote: an independent, "homegrown" regional order would deliver peace and security
insights.locator: paragraph on Qalibaf's regional security remarks

insights.claim: Six months into the war (started February 28, 2026), neither side is firing on the other but neither is pursuing peace talks, leaving the conflict in a frozen, high-risk stalemate.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: A frozen-but-unresolved conflict sustains elevated geopolitical risk premia in oil and regional equities indefinitely, since there's no clear near-term catalyst for either escalation or resolution.
insights.quote: the sides are not firing at each other but also showing no sign of pursuing peace talks

insights.claim: Trump has not achieved his stated war objectives of dismantling Iran's nuclear program or triggering an Iranian uprising against the clerical government, and the actual state of Iran's nuclear program is uncertain because UN inspectors have been shut out since 2025.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Loss of IAEA-style verification means markets cannot rely on official assessments of Iran's nuclear status, adding an information-void risk premium to any Iran-related trade or policy forecast.
insights.quote: dismantling Iran's nuclear programme - the state of which remains uncertain given that U.N. inspectors have been shut out since 2025

insights.claim: The war has killed thousands, mainly in Iran, including 168 Iranian schoolchildren on the first day of the war (February 28, 2026), while the US has reported over 750 military personnel wounded and 18 killed.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: The scale and civilian nature of casualties (including 168 schoolchildren) raises the political cost for the US of continuing the campaign and strengthens Iran's diplomatic narrative internationally.
insights.quote: Thousands have been killed, mainly in Iran, where 168 Iranian school children were killed on the first day of the war. The U.S. has reported more than 750 military personnel wounded and 18 killed.

insights.claim: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian called for a diplomatic solution while framing Iran as currently negotiating from a position of strength and moral high ground over US strikes on schools, hospitals and infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Pezeshkian's framing signals Iran's civilian leadership wants an exit but is conditioning it on being seen to negotiate from strength, meaning a deal is more likely once Iran can claim a face-saving narrative rather than under pure sanctions pressure.
insights.quote: It would be better to end the war today, when we are powerful and have dignity, and the whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasizes that America, contrary to all regulations, attacked our schools, hospitals, and infrastructure and is hated in the world
insights.locator: closing quote from Pezeshkian via ISNA
